screens.title: Resiliency and High Availability with Direct Connect
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on building Direct Connect designs that survive real failures. You will learn why redundancy is not just an option but a requirement for enterprise hybrid connectivity, and how small design choices — different locations, diverse physical paths, separate routers, and BGP tuning — change whether traffic keeps flowing during an outage. We will also cover faster failure detection with BFD and practical testing steps you can repeat in maintenance windows. A concrete example you will revisit is a pair of Direct Connects terminating on two on‑premises routers where AS_PATH prepending on the secondary creates an active/standby inbound preference. Finally, we discuss common mistakes such as hidden single points of failure in the “last mile” and under-tested failover procedures. By the end you should be able to list the core components of a highly available Direct Connect setup, propose multiple redundancy strategies, and describe how BGP and BFD interact during a failure. Consider what single component in your network would break connectivity today — that is the starting point for redesign.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Resiliency and High Availability
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Resiliency and High Availability with Direct Connect

Build Direct Connect solutions that tolerate link, router, and location failures. Learn physical and routing controls to keep traffic flowing.

In this lesson

N+1 redundancy, diverse paths, BGP AS_PATH prepending, BFD acceleration, and repeatable failover tests.

Why it matters

Downtime from a single Direct Connect failure can disrupt critical workloads; layered redundancy limits blast radius and speeds recovery.

Explore Key Topics
N+1 Redundancy
Add at least one extra connection beyond your needs to tolerate failures.
BGP Traffic Engineering
Use AS_PATH prepending to influence inbound traffic preference from AWS.
Failover Testing
Run planned simulations, monitor route tables, and validate application behavior.
Architecture snapshot
Concept cards
Two DX Locations
Separate colocation sites protect against a single location outage.
Path Diversity
Different fiber conduits and carrier circuits reduce common-mode failures.
Separate Routers
Terminate DX on distinct customer routers to avoid a router S.P.O.F.
BGP Controls
AS_PATH prepending and BFD let you influence and accelerate failover behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives focus your work on the resilient parts of a Direct Connect design. First, you will identify the critical components of a highly available Direct Connect architecture. That means recognizing locations, routers, physical cross‑connects, and BGP sessions that must be protected. Second, you will design redundant Direct Connect connections using diverse paths and multiple locations. This objective stresses physical diversity: different Direct Connect locations, separate fiber routes, and different carrier circuits. Both objectives are practical — you should be able to point to a diagram and explain which element would fail and why your design prevents total loss. A simple example to keep in mind is two Direct Connects in different cities terminating on separate on‑premises routers. If one city loses power, the other still carries traffic. Finally, use the verification milestone attached to each card to confirm competency during design reviews or lab simulations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Implementation & Validation
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide drills into implementation skills and validation practice you must master. You will learn how to implement AS_PATH prepending to make a secondary Direct Connect less preferred for inbound traffic, and how to enable BFD to reduce detection time for link or router failures. Both are operational skills: AS_PATH prepending requires a route‑map on the router advertising your prefixes; BFD requires configuration with your BGP peer so both sides agree on rapid failure detection. Finally, you will implement test procedures to validate failover. Tests might be administrative BGP shutdowns, simulated cross‑connect removals with coordination, or controlled router reboots. For each test you should capture route table changes and application latency. Successful mastery means you can not only configure the mechanics but also interpret show command outputs and document recovery steps.

screens.title: N+1 Redundancy: the foundation
screens.narratorSegment: N+1 redundancy means provisioning at least one more component than required to meet normal demand. In Direct Connect designs that often translates to two connections when one satisfies bandwidth, or two locations when one meets latency goals. The idea is simple: if an active element fails, the extra element can carry traffic while you repair the failed piece. A concrete example is a production line using a 10 gigabit Direct Connect; instead of a single 10 G circuit, you might provision two 10 G connections with traffic engineering so either can carry the full load during a failure. N+1 is not a license to ignore capacity planning—make sure your backup path can truly handle worst‑case load, or implement graceful degradation policies at the application tier. A common misconception is thinking that two links in the same conduit or same router equal redundancy; they do not. True N+1 requires independent failure domains: different physical routes, separate carrier termination points, or distinct routers. When documenting an N+1 design, list the failure domain for each component and the recovery action. That practice helps teams avoid hidden single points of failure and provides clear operational steps during an incident.

keyIdea.title: N+1 summary
keyIdea.text: Provision one additional independent component so a single failure does not interrupt service; ensure the spare can handle required load.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › N+1 Redundancy
Definition

N+1 redundancy provides one spare component above operational needs so that a single failure does not cause a service outage.

Why it matters: avoids single point failures in transport and termination equipment.
Sizing note: ensure spare can carry peak load or implement degradation rules at application layer.
Documentation: list failure domain and recovery action for each component.
Concrete example
Two 10 G Direct Connects
Primary carries production traffic. Secondary is configured to be capable of handling the full 10 G during failover. Traffic engineering makes the primary preferred for inbound traffic.
Key Takeaway

N+1 is effective only if the spare is independent and can carry required load when needed.

Common mistake
Two circuits that share the same conduit or router are not true N+1. Confirm physical independence.

screens.title: Designing Diverse Paths and Locations
screens.narratorSegment: Designing diversity requires thinking in failure domains. Start by choosing Direct Connect locations that are geographically and facility-separate. If your primary DX is in Ashburn, choose a secondary in a different city and, if possible, a different colocation provider. Next, verify path diversity: ensure cross‑connects, carrier circuits, and metro fiber routes do not share the same physical conduit or meet at the same distribution frame. The colocation provider can usually provide path reports; ask for distinct fiber handoffs and separate carrier IDs. At the on‑premises end, terminate connections on separate routers in different racks with separate power circuits to remove single points of failure. A simple process flow to validate diversity includes: 1) list components and their physical dependencies; 2) request path diversity confirmation from carriers; 3) map termination racks and power feeds; 4) implement BGP sessions from each router; 5) run failover tests. A common misconception is relying solely on logical separation such as VLANs without physical path separation. Logical isolation helps, but cannot protect against a cable cut. Always document diversity and include it in your runbook and change control.

keyIdea.title: Diversity checklist
keyIdea.text: Treat locations, fiber routes, carriers, racks, and power as separate failure domains and validate each with providers and on‑site inspections.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Designing Diverse Paths
Validation process
  1. Inventory DX locations, carrier circuits, and cross‑connect IDs.
  2. Request separate cable paths and carrier termination points.
  3. Terminate on separate on‑prem racks and routers with independent power.
  4. Establish independent BGP sessions and review route advertisements.
  5. Run simulated failover tests and record outcomes.
Use this flow as a checklist during design reviews with carriers and colocation teams.
Example scenario
Primary: DX-A (Ashburn) — Carrier X
Secondary: DX-B (Miami) — Carrier Y with different fiber route. On‑prem termination on Router1 and Router2 in separate racks.
Key Takeaway

Physical diversity is the most effective mitigation against common‑mode failures; verify with providers.

Pro tip
Request carrier path documentation and put it in your runbook to prevent assumptions about diversity.

screens.title: Terminating on Different Routers and Avoiding S.P.O.F.
screens.narratorSegment: Terminating Direct Connect connections on separate routers is a low‑effort, high‑impact resilience improvement. If both DX connections land on the same router, that router becomes a single point of failure regardless of how diverse your fiber is. For robust resilience, place each DX termination on a distinct customer router, ideally in different racks and fed by separate power circuits. Also ensure distinct control‑plane elements such as separate router supervisors or cards if your hardware supports them. Operationally, configure each router with its own BGP session to AWS and advertise the same prefixes so AWS learns both paths. Keep the configuration consistent but avoid identical hardware dependencies. A known misconception is that identical configurations across routers create unnecessary symmetry; rather, align policies but verify separate hardware and maintenance windows so you do not patch both routers simultaneously without planning. Include rack-level diagrams and power circuit IDs in your runbook so field teams know which components to isolate during maintenance. This planning reduces human error and speeds recovery during incidents. Terminating on Different Routers and Avoiding S.P.O.F. means terminate dx on separate routers and power feeds to eliminate the router as a single point of failure.. In practical terms, how router placement and rack design reduce single points of failure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Router Termination
Architecture pattern
Terminate each Direct Connect on a different customer router in separate racks. Use separate UPS or power circuits to minimize correlated failures.
Ensure independent BGP sessions from each router with consistent prefix advertisement.
Label rack IDs, router serials, and power circuit IDs in the runbook and on diagrams.
Concrete scenario
Router A (rack 10, power A) — DX1
Router B (rack 12, power B) — DX2. Each router peers with AWS over separate VIFs and advertises identical prefixes.
Key Takeaway

Router separation reduces a common hardware or software failure from taking both DX links down.

screens.title: AS_PATH Prepending for Inbound Traffic Engineering
screens.narratorSegment: AS_PATH prepending is a straightforward BGP technique to influence inbound traffic. BGP selects paths with the shortest AS_PATH, so if you prepend your own ASN multiple times on the secondary advertisement, that path appears longer and AWS will prefer the primary. Practically, you implement a route‑map on the router that adds your ASN three or four times to the AS_PATH for prefixes advertised over the secondary VIF. The result is an active/standby inbound preference: AWS sends traffic to the primary unless it becomes unavailable. A common misconception is thinking AS_PATH prepending controls outbound traffic; it only affects how remote peers choose routes toward you. Outbound decisions are influenced by local preference and routing policy. Below is a conceptual snippet that you will use in labs: it shows router BGP configuration for two routers and a route‑map that prepends the ASN. When testing, run show commands to confirm the AS_PATH length changes and that AWS switches to the secondary when the primary BGP session is withdrawn. Always document the change so operators understand its intent. AS_PATH Prepending for Inbound Traffic Engineering means prepend your asn on the secondary path so remote peers prefer the primary under normal conditions; monitor as_path lengths to verify behavior.. In practical terms, how to make the secondary path less preferred using as_path modification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: AS_PATH use
keyIdea.text: Prepend your ASN on the secondary path so remote peers prefer the primary under normal conditions; monitor AS_PATH lengths to verify behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › AS_PATH Prepending
Concept

Add your ASN multiple times to the AS_PATH on the secondary route advertisement to make that path look longer and less preferred by AWS.

Remember: this affects inbound traffic from AWS to your network, not your outbound selection.
Check your work
  • Verify BGP AS_PATH length on AWS-visible routes.
  • Confirm primary path has shorter AS_PATH under normal operation.
  • Simulate primary failure and verify AWS switches to secondary.
Conceptual BGP snippet
router bgp 65000
 neighbor <AWS_IP_PRIMARY> remote-as 64512
  address-family ipv4
   network 172.16.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0
  exit-address-family

router bgp 65000
 neighbor <AWS_IP_SECONDARY> remote-as 64512
  address-family ipv4
   network 172.16.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0
   neighbor <AWS_IP_SECONDARY> route-map PREPEND_AS out
  exit-address-family

route-map PREPEND_AS permit 10
 set as-path prepend 65000 65000 65000
Replace placeholder IPs with your DX peer addresses during lab configuration. Capture show ip bgp output to confirm AS_PATH updates.

screens.title: BFD and Fast Failure Detection
screens.narratorSegment: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, or BFD, is a lightweight protocol designed to detect link or neighbor failures faster than standard BGP keepalives. BFD operates at the forwarding plane and can detect failures in sub‑second intervals depending on timers, which shortens the window during which traffic blackholes or slow reconvergence occur. For Direct Connect, enabling BFD on VIFs expedites the withdrawal of routes when a peer or link fails, allowing the redundant path to carry traffic sooner. A concrete example: if BGP keepalives default to tens of seconds, an outage could disrupt sensitive traffic; configuring BFD with aggressive intervals can reduce detection to well under a second. A key misconception is thinking BFD replaces BGP; it does not. BFD only signals that a path is down faster; BGP still performs route exchange and selection. When enabling BFD, coordinate with the AWS side and carriers as needed and test with controlled failovers. Record convergence times before and after enabling BFD so you can quantify the benefit for your applications. BFD and Fast Failure Detection means bfd speeds failure detection to sub‑second ranges and should be combined with bgp for faster failover.. In practical terms, how bidirectional forwarding detection accelerates failover. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: BFD in short
keyIdea.text: BFD speeds failure detection to sub‑second ranges and should be combined with BGP for faster failover.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › BFD — Fast Detection
What BFD does

BFD provides rapid detection of forwarding plane failures and notifies control protocols like BGP so they can withdraw routes quickly.

Benefit: sub‑second detection reduces outage time for sensitive applications.
Compatibility: BFD works alongside BGP; both must be configured and tested together.
Testing BFD
  1. Enable BFD on both BGP peers and verify session establishment.
  2. Record baseline convergence time without BFD by simulating link down.
  3. Enable BFD with conservative timers, retest, and measure reduced convergence.
Key Takeaway

BFD dramatically shortens detection time but must be validated and coordinated with AWS and carriers.

screens.title: Failover Testing: a repeatable approach
screens.narratorSegment: Failover testing is essential to confirm that your redundancy works as designed. Start by creating a test plan that defines scope, safety, and rollback steps. Include which BGP sessions will be taken down, whether you will shut an interface or simulate a cross‑connect removal, the monitoring to capture, and the expected outcomes. Schedule a maintenance window and notify stakeholders. During the test, collect BGP neighbor status, route tables, VPC routing entries, and application metrics like latency and error rates. A practical sequence is: 1) baseline capture; 2) gracefully administratively shut down the BGP neighbor on the primary router; 3) observe route withdrawals and verify traffic shift to secondary; 4) restore the primary and validate reconvergence. For more realistic tests coordinate with your colocation provider before physical disconnects. Common mistakes include not measuring application impact or not having a documented rollback, which can turn a test into an outage. After the test, produce a short report documenting timings, observed behavior, and recommended changes. Regular, incremental tests build confidence and refine runbooks. Failover Testing: a repeatable approach means a documented, repeatable test plan with baselines, controlled failure injection, and measured outcomes proves redundancy in practice.. In practical terms, how to plan, execute, and validate failover tests safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Failover Testing
Test plan checklist
  • Define scope, safety, and rollback steps.
  • Capture baselines: BGP state, route tables, application metrics.
  • Simulate failure: BGP shutdown, interface down, or coordinated physical disconnect.
  • Observe convergence and application behavior; document times.
  • Restore and verify normal operation; write a short test report.
Example test script
Step A:
Record show ip bgp and application latency for 5 minutes.
Step B:
Administratively shut down primary BGP neighbor and time convergence.
Step C:
Restore BGP and confirm route preferences and application recovery.
Key Takeaway

Test in a controlled manner, measure, and document. Tests reveal hidden dependencies and validate runbooks.

screens.title: Active/Passive vs Active/Active Direct Connect
screens.narratorSegment: Active/passive and active/active are two operational patterns for using multiple Direct Connects. In active/passive, the primary path is preferred and carries most inbound traffic while the secondary is standby and used only during failures. AS_PATH prepending is an easy way to achieve active/passive inbound preference. This pattern is predictable and often simpler to troubleshoot. Active/active uses both connections simultaneously, possibly splitting traffic for capacity or redundancy. Active/active requires careful load distribution, consistent routing policies, and awareness of how AWS and your network perform equal-cost or policy-based balancing. A misconception is assuming active/active always doubles throughput; in many cases one path may still carry more traffic due to BGP path selection rules. Another tradeoff is failover behavior: active/passive gives clear deterministic behavior when the primary fails, while active/active requires ensuring either path can carry the full load during a failure. Active/Passive
Primary preferred; secondary used on failover. Easier to reason about inbound traffic using AS_PATH prepending.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Even carefully planned designs can suffer from avoidable mistakes. One frequent pitfall is lack of true diversity: having two Direct Connects that share a conduit, meet at the same distribution point, or terminate on the same router. Another is incorrect BGP configuration such as misapplied AS_PATH prepending or forgetting to announce the same prefixes on both routers. Not enabling BFD when your applications require fast recovery is another oversight. Operationally, insufficient testing is common; teams often assume failover works and never run full simulations that include application behavior. Finally, ignoring the last mile — the carrier or data center handoff — leaves you exposed to cable cuts and provider incidents. To avoid these mistakes, maintain a physical path inventory, review BGP configs during change control, enable BFD when appropriate, and schedule recurring failover tests with documented rollback procedures. Teach your operations team the recovery steps and include runbook checklists for each failure type. Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Hands-on Activity
Task checklist
  1. Write BGP neighbor and network statements for Router A and Router B advertising 172.16.0.0/16.
  2. On Router B create route-map PREPEND_AS and set as-path prepend 65000 65000 65000.
  3. Confirm AS_PATH lengths via show ip bgp on both routers and on any BGP monitor.

  5. Document outputs and expected recovery actions in your test report.
Starter configuration (conceptual)
# Router A (Primary DX)
router bgp 65000
 neighbor <AWS_IP_PRIMARY> remote-as 64512
  address-family ipv4
   network 172.16.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0
  exit-address-family

# Router B (Secondary DX)
router bgp 65000
 neighbor <AWS_IP_SECONDARY> remote-as 64512
  address-family ipv4
   network 172.16.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0
   neighbor <AWS_IP_SECONDARY> route-map PREPEND_AS out
  exit-address-family

route-map PREPEND_AS permit 10
 set as-path prepend 65000 65000 65000
Replace <AWS_IP_PRIMARY> and <AWS_IP_SECONDARY> with peer IPs. Capture show ip bgp and peer states before and after tests.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on building Direct Connect designs that survive real failures. You will learn why redundancy is not just an option but a requirement for enterprise hybrid connectivity, and how small design choices — different locations, diverse physical paths, separate routers, and BGP tuning — change whether traffic keeps flowing during an outage. We will also cover faster failure detection with BFD and practical testing steps you can repeat in maintenance windows. A concrete example you will revisit is a pair of Direct Connects terminating on two on‑premises routers where AS_PATH prepending on the secondary creates an active/standby inbound preference. Finally, we discuss common mistakes such as hidden single points of failure in the “last mile” and under-tested failover procedures. By the end you should be able to list the core components of a highly available Direct Connect setup, propose multiple redundancy strategies, and describe how BGP and BFD interact during a failure. Consider what single component in your network would break connectivity today — that is the starting point for redesign.

These learning objectives focus your work on the resilient parts of a Direct Connect design. First, you will identify the critical components of a highly available Direct Connect architecture. That means recognizing locations, routers, physical cross‑connects, and BGP sessions that must be protected. Second, you will design redundant Direct Connect connections using diverse paths and multiple locations. This objective stresses physical diversity: different Direct Connect locations, separate fiber routes, and different carrier circuits. Both objectives are practical — you should be able to point to a diagram and explain which element would fail and why your design prevents total loss. A simple example to keep in mind is two Direct Connects in different cities terminating on separate on‑premises routers. If one city loses power, the other still carries traffic. Finally, use the verification milestone attached to each card to confirm competency during design reviews or lab simulations.

This second objectives slide drills into implementation skills and validation practice you must master. You will learn how to implement AS_PATH prepending to make a secondary Direct Connect less preferred for inbound traffic, and how to enable BFD to reduce detection time for link or router failures. Both are operational skills: AS_PATH prepending requires a route‑map on the router advertising your prefixes; BFD requires configuration with your BGP peer so both sides agree on rapid failure detection. Finally, you will implement test procedures to validate failover. Tests might be administrative BGP shutdowns, simulated cross‑connect removals with coordination, or controlled router reboots. For each test you should capture route table changes and application latency. Successful mastery means you can not only configure the mechanics but also interpret show command outputs and document recovery steps.

N+1 redundancy means provisioning at least one more component than required to meet normal demand. In Direct Connect designs that often translates to two connections when one satisfies bandwidth, or two locations when one meets latency goals. The idea is simple: if an active element fails, the extra element can carry traffic while you repair the failed piece. A concrete example is a production line using a 10 gigabit Direct Connect; instead of a single 10 G circuit, you might provision two 10 G connections with traffic engineering so either can carry the full load during a failure. N+1 is not a license to ignore capacity planning—make sure your backup path can truly handle worst‑case load, or implement graceful degradation policies at the application tier. A common misconception is thinking that two links in the same conduit or same router equal redundancy; they do not. True N+1 requires independent failure domains: different physical routes, separate carrier termination points, or distinct routers. When documenting an N+1 design, list the failure domain for each component and the recovery action. That practice helps teams avoid hidden single points of failure and provides clear operational steps during an incident.

Designing diversity requires thinking in failure domains. Start by choosing Direct Connect locations that are geographically and facility-separate. If your primary DX is in Ashburn, choose a secondary in a different city and, if possible, a different colocation provider. Next, verify path diversity: ensure cross‑connects, carrier circuits, and metro fiber routes do not share the same physical conduit or meet at the same distribution frame. The colocation provider can usually provide path reports; ask for distinct fiber handoffs and separate carrier IDs. At the on‑premises end, terminate connections on separate routers in different racks with separate power circuits to remove single points of failure. A simple process flow to validate diversity includes: 1) list components and their physical dependencies; 2) request path diversity confirmation from carriers; 3) map termination racks and power feeds; 4) implement BGP sessions from each router; 5) run failover tests. A common misconception is relying solely on logical separation such as VLANs without physical path separation. Logical isolation helps, but cannot protect against a cable cut. Always document diversity and include it in your runbook and change control.

Terminating Direct Connect connections on separate routers is a low‑effort, high‑impact resilience improvement. If both DX connections land on the same router, that router becomes a single point of failure regardless of how diverse your fiber is. For robust resilience, place each DX termination on a distinct customer router, ideally in different racks and fed by separate power circuits. Also ensure distinct control‑plane elements such as separate router supervisors or cards if your hardware supports them. Operationally, configure each router with its own BGP session to AWS and advertise the same prefixes so AWS learns both paths. Keep the configuration consistent but avoid identical hardware dependencies. A known misconception is that identical configurations across routers create unnecessary symmetry; rather, align policies but verify separate hardware and maintenance windows so you do not patch both routers simultaneously without planning. Include rack-level diagrams and power circuit IDs in your runbook so field teams know which components to isolate during maintenance. This planning reduces human error and speeds recovery during incidents. In practical terms, how router placement and rack design reduce single points of failure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AS_PATH prepending is a straightforward BGP technique to influence inbound traffic. BGP selects paths with the shortest AS_PATH, so if you prepend your own ASN multiple times on the secondary advertisement, that path appears longer and AWS will prefer the primary. Practically, you implement a route‑map on the router that adds your ASN three or four times to the AS_PATH for prefixes advertised over the secondary VIF. The result is an active/standby inbound preference: AWS sends traffic to the primary unless it becomes unavailable. BFD operates at the forwarding plane and can detect failures in sub‑second intervals depending on timers, which shortens the window during which traffic blackholes or slow reconvergence occur. For Direct Connect, enabling BFD on VIFs expedites the withdrawal of routes when a peer or link fails, allowing the redundant path to carry traffic sooner. Record convergence times before and after enabling BFD so you can quantify the benefit for your applications.
